newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Afghan opposition said agreeable to truce demands.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition said agreeable to truce demands.

text.p: A Pakistani peace emissary said on Thursday the Afghan opposition alliance appears agreeable to the Taleban militia's ceasefire demands but the two sides remain at odds over achieving peace.
A senior Pakistan Foreign Ministry official, Iftikhar Murshed, told reporters after talks with the warring sides that Islamabad would continue efforts towards peace talks.
He said he met the opposition representatives in the northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Tuesday and had the impression that "they are agreeable to a ceasefire".
"They said 'If the other side stops fighting, we will also stop fighting'," Murshed said.

He said a ceasefire and exchange of prisoners were pre-conditions set by the Taleban in a meeting with him on June 21 to meet opposition demands for a political commission to consider establishing a broad-based Afghan government.
But the opposition alliance seemed reluctant to release captured Taleban fighters, fearing they would return to warfare, Murshed said.

However, the opposition agreed to consider a Pakistani suggestion to release, as a goodwill gesture, former Taleban foreign minister Mullah Mohammad Ghous and central bank chief Mullah Ahsanullah, Murshed added.
The two were arrested in Mazar-i-Sharif by opposition leader General Abdul Malik's forces in late May.
Murshed said the Taleban rejected an opposition demand to demilitarise the capital Kabul for a political commission meeting.

Instead, he said, the Taleban suggested the commission meet in Islamabad, where Pakistan has offered to host the intra-Afghan dialogue with the participation of Afghanistan's immediate neighbours as well as the United States and Russia.
Murshed said he had also met ousted Afghan president Burhanuddin Rabbani in Mazar-i-Sharif before his talks with an opposition alliance team led by General Malik.
Previously, he met Taleban officials in Kandahar on June 21 and opposition representatives in Dubai on June 18-19.

Pakistan recognised the Taleban government in late May after the purist Islamic militia briefly captured Mazar-i-Sharif with Malik's help and was followed by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Ethnic Uzbek and Tajik opposition factions accuse Islamabad of helping the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban, who control more than two-thirds of Afghanistan after capturing Kabul last September.
The Taleban want Malik to free hundreds of Taleban fighters captured in Mazar-i-Sharif.
